title: Med Spa Membership Price Increase: How to Raise Prices on Existing Members (October 2026)
summary: How to run a med spa membership price increase: grandfather rules, notice periods, failed-payment handling and a member script that keeps people enrolled.
body_markdown:
## When a Med Spa Membership Price Increase Is Justified


A membership price increase is justified when the margin on a tier has dropped below what you priced it for, usually because product cost, labor or included-service volume moved. Do the math on one tier before you touch anything: member fee on one side, the cost of the services and discounts that member actually redeems on the other.


The pattern is a common one. The membership launched with a few benefits, then credits, rollover and a birthday perk got added one at a time, and nobody repriced. If your[membership pricing](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-pricing-retention) was set against competitors rather than your own cost basis, an increase is a correction, not a favor you are asking for. Pull your breakage and redemption numbers from[practice analytics](https://decodahealth.com/products/analytics) before you pick a number, since members who use every credit are the ones the old price hurts you on.


## What Your Membership Agreement Lets You Change


The signed agreement is the answer to whether you can raise a member's price, and it should be the first document you open. Three clauses matter: the term, the price-change language, and the cancellation notice.


Operators run into trouble because most memberships behave like contracts in the patient's mind even when the paperwork is thin. A patient who joined at $149 with a 12-month term has a reasonable expectation of $149 for 12 months. A month-to-month member has agreed to less, but still agreed to a specific number.


Agreement says What you can usually do Safer move


Fixed term (for example 12 months) with a stated price Raise the price at renewal only Send the new price 60 days before the term ends


Month-to-month with a clause allowing changes on notice Raise the price after the notice period 30 to 60 days' written notice, with a cancel-anytime reminder


Month-to-month, silent on price changes Raise only with the member's agreement Ask members to accept the new terms before the next bill


Annual prepay Keep the paid year intact, change price at renewal Offer to lock the old rate if they renew early


Have a healthcare or consumer attorney check the clause that governs changes. If you are rewriting the agreement anyway, add price-change language for new signups now, so the next increase is simpler.


## Grandfathering Existing Members: Forever, Timed or Not at All


Grandfathering means existing members keep their signup price while new members pay the new one. A time-limited legacy rate is usually the right default, because permanent grandfathering lets the pricing gap widen every year.


Three approaches cover nearly every case:


- **Permanent grandfathering.** Zero cancellations from the increase, because there is no increase. The cost is a growing share of members paying below your current margin.
- **Timed grandfathering.** The old price holds for 6 to 12 months, then moves to the new price on a date you announce up front. Most owners land here.
- **Step-up.** Legacy members move to a midpoint price now, and to full price at the next renewal. This suits a large gap between old and new.


A common middle path is permanent grandfathering for a small founding group and a time limit for everyone after. That is a defensible policy as long as you write it down and tell people. A founding-member rate that quietly applies to some people and not others is the version that causes arguments at the front desk.


## How Much Notice to Give, and What Auto-Renewal Law Adds


Give month-to-month members at least 30 days' written notice before a higher price bills, and give anyone on a fixed term notice before the term ends. Those numbers are practice norms, not statutes, so your agreement and your state set the true minimum.


The legal layer is real. The FTC enforces disclosure of material terms and simple cancellation for recurring charges under the[Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/statutes/restore-online-shoppers-confidence-act) , and that enforcement continued after the Click to Cancel rule was vacated, as this[Holland & Knight summary of subscription enforcement](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/09/ftc-steps-up-subscription-enforcement-after-click-to-cancel-rule) explains. States add their own rules. California's amended automatic renewal law took effect July 1, 2025 and requires clear and conspicuous notice of material changes, as described in this[Kilpatrick Townsend alert on the July 2025 amendments](https://ktslaw.com/en/Insights/Alert/2024/10/California-Latest-Automatic-Renewal-Law-Amendments-Take-Effect-in-July-2025) . A price change is a material change.


The practical rule: send the notice early, keep a record of when and how each member received it, and make cancelling as easy as joining. If a member can sign up in a form, they should be able to cancel without a phone call. The same discipline matters on the[new med spa laws](https://decodahealth.com/blog/new-med-spa-laws) your state may be adding this year.


## Handling Failed Payments Before and After the Change


Decide how a failed membership payment works before the increase goes live, because a price change makes failures more likely and recovery messier. A member whose card declines at the new price is a different problem from one whose card expired in March.


Write the rule in four lines: how many retry attempts, over how many days, whether benefits stay usable during that window, and what happens at the end. Some operators allow a 30-day grace period after a membership ends so a lapsed member can still use paid credits, which keeps goodwill and reduces disputes. Others pause benefits on the first failed charge. Either works if members know it in advance.


The trap sits in recovery. Collecting an overdue renewal can move the member's billing date, and in some systems it bills the missed month and the next month together. Run one test account through a decline, a retry and a successful recovery before you roll the change out to everyone, and check the invoice dates and totals by hand. Our guide to[med spa failed membership payments](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-failed-membership-payments) covers the retry schedule and grace period in full. Reconciling these exceptions is where[med spa billing software](https://decodahealth.com/products/billing) earns its cost.


## Writing the Member Announcement


The announcement works when the first two sentences state the new price and the date it starts. Members read a vague "we're making some changes" email as bad news and then hunt for the number.


Here is a structure that holds up:


1. **Price and date first.** "Starting December 1, the Gold membership moves from $249 to $279 per month."
2. **What they keep.** Rollover, perks and any benefit you are adding at the same time.
3. **One choice.** Lock the current rate for 12 months by switching to annual billing, or stay month to month at the new price.
4. **How to cancel.** Say it plainly and link it. Hiding the exit raises disputes and breaks the consent rules above.


Send it by email and text, post it at the front desk, and brief staff on a two-sentence answer to "why now." Reasons that hold up are specific: product costs rose, you are adding a visit or credit, the price has not moved since launch. Apologizing at length signals that the price is negotiable, which it should not be once policy is set.


## Modeling Cancellations and Protecting Revenue


Model the increase as revenue gained minus revenue lost to the members who leave. If a $30 increase on 100 members risks 5 cancellations at $249, you gain $2,750 a month net, but the 5 members who leave were also buying injectables, so count their add-on spend too.


Plan for a small group to cancel and treat each one as a conversation. A member who cancels over price will sometimes accept a lower tier or a pause for two months. Offer that before the cancellation processes, and track where members land after the change: stayed, downgraded, paused, left. Compare the next 90 days to the 90 days before.


Timing matters too. A notice that lands in a slow month can fold into your normal[seasonal cash flow](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-seasonal-cash-flow-planning) without a visible dip, while one sent right before a holiday promotion competes with the offer. Pair the increase with something members can see, like a new perk, and it stops feeling like a pure price move. For a longevity or hormone program with premium pricing, the[longevity membership premium pricing](https://decodahealth.com/blog/longevity-membership-premium-pricing) approach shows how to frame the value of a tier.


## Questions to Ask Your Software Before You Change a Price


Before you edit a membership plan, find out whether the edit applies to current members, new members or both, and how member pricing interacts with your[promotion and stacking rules](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-discount-policy) . Platforms differ here, and finding out after you click save is expensive.


Ask your vendor, in writing:


- If I change the price on a plan, does it change for people already enrolled?
- Can I keep specific members at their old price, and can I set an end date for that?
- When a member changes tier or payment method, does the billing date move?
- Can one patient hold two memberships and pay once at checkout?
- How are unused credits and rollover shown on the liability report?


Owners who ask these after the change, not before, tend to find the answers mid-increase. Ask every vendor, ours included, to show each one on a demo call instead of assuming. The setup guide for[VIP memberships, beauty banks and patient wallets](https://decodahealth.com/blog/setting-up-vip-memberships-beauty-banks-and-patient-wallets) covers the credit side of the same problem.

## Final Thoughts on Raising Membership Prices Without Losing Members


A membership price increase goes well when the agreement supports it, the notice is early, the failed-payment rule is written and the first email states the number. Start with one tier this week: pull its margin, read its agreement, and pick the date. ## Frequently Asked Questions


Can a med spa raise the price of a membership for existing members?


Yes, as long as your signed agreement allows it and you give notice before the new price bills. If the agreement fixes the price for a term, the increase waits until that term ends. If it says nothing, treat the old price as protected until renewal and get written agreement for any change.


How much notice should a med spa give before raising membership prices?


Thirty days is a common floor for month-to-month members, and many operators give 60 days to anyone on a longer term. Your agreement and your state's auto-renewal law set the real minimum, so check both before you pick a date. A longer window also gives members time to book the benefits they have already paid for.


Should I grandfather existing members at their old price?


Grandfather for a defined period rather than forever. A time-limited legacy rate, such as 6 to 12 months, protects trust with your most loyal members while stopping the gap between old and new prices from widening each year. Permanent grandfathering is only worth it for a small founding group you want to reward on purpose.


What happens to a membership when a payment fails after a price change?


The failed charge needs a written rule before it happens: how many retries, how many days of grace, and whether benefits pause. Recovering an overdue payment can move the billing date or bill the old and new price together, so test that sequence on one account before you change every member.


Do membership price increases have to be disclosed under auto-renewal laws?


Material changes to an auto-renewing plan, including price, generally need clear notice before they take effect. California's amended automatic renewal law, effective July 1, 2025, is the strictest example, and the FTC enforces similar disclosure expectations under ROSCA. Have a healthcare or consumer attorney review your notice language.


How do I tell members about a price increase without losing them?


Lead with what they keep, state the new price and effective date in the first two sentences, and offer one concrete choice such as locking the current rate for a year by moving to annual billing. Send it by email and text, then have the front desk mention it at checkout. Expect a small group to cancel and plan the budget around that.
